title: Chicken Adobo
description: Chicken braised in soy sauce, vinegar, garlic and bay leaf until the sauce turns glossy and dark — the everyday dinner every Filipino household makes differently.

ingredients.item: bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks, cut into serving pieces

ingredients.note: cane vinegar is milder; start with less if using distilled white vinegar

steps: Combine the chicken, soy sauce and crushed garlic in a bowl; massage well and marinate at least 1 hour, longer if possible.
Lift the chicken out of the marinade, keeping both the garlicky liquid and the pieces of garlic to use later.
Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and pan-fry the chicken 2 minutes per side until lightly browned; remove and set aside.
Add the remaining oil to the same pot and sauté the reserved garlic until fragrant and starting to brown.
Return the chicken to the pot with the reserved marinade, peppercorns, bay leaves and water; bring to a boil, then cover and simmer 30 minutes until tender.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil uncovered, without stirring, for 2 minutes so it loses its raw sharpness.
Stir and simmer uncovered another 15 minutes until the sauce reduces and turns glossy.
Stir in the sugar and salt to taste, then turn off the heat and serve hot with rice.
tips: Do not stir after adding the vinegar until it has boiled for at least 2 minutes, or the sauce tastes raw and sharp.
Marinating overnight (unattended, in the fridge) deepens the flavour more than a rushed 30 minutes.
Adobo tastes better the next day — make it ahead and reheat gently.
nutritionNote: Salty and rich from soy sauce and rendered chicken fat; balance with steamed vegetables or a fresh tomato-cucumber side and go light on extra rice or soy sauce at the table.

title: Pork Sinigang
description: Pork ribs and vegetables simmered in a sour tamarind broth — the pucker-inducing soup Filipinos crave on rainy days and reach for when someone's under the weather.

ingredients.item: pork spare ribs, cut into 2-inch pieces

ingredients.note: adds aroma, not real heat; leave out entirely for a milder pot
or 15 pieces fresh tamarind pods, boiled soft and strained, for a more traditional sour base

steps: Rinse the pork ribs and place in a large pot; cover with the water and bring to a boil over medium heat, skimming off the scum that rises.
Once the broth runs clear, add the tomatoes, onion and fish sauce; lower the heat and simmer 45-60 minutes, covered, until the pork is fork-tender.
Add the taro and cook 5-6 minutes until it starts to soften and lightly thickens the broth.
Stir in the tamarind soup base until dissolved, then taste — the broth should be assertively sour.
Add the radish and chilies; simmer 3 minutes.
Add the long beans, eggplant and okra; cook 3-4 minutes until just tender but not mushy.
Season with salt and pepper to taste, then add the bok choy and cook 1 minute more, just until wilted.
Remove from the heat right away, since bok choy overcooks fast, and serve hot in bowls with steamed rice.
tips: Parboil-and-discard the first pork water for a cleaner, less cloudy broth if you have the time.
Add vegetables in order of cook time — roots first, leafy greens last — so nothing turns to mush.
The broth should taste sour before you add salt; sinigang is meant to pucker slightly.
kidNote: Ladle the kids' broth before adding the whole chilies, and go a little lighter on the tamarind base in their portion if they're sensitive to sour — pork, taro and soft vegetables over rice is usually an easy sell.
nutritionNote: A vegetable-packed, comparatively lean soup once you skim the fat; the broth alone is fairly low in carbohydrate, so a normal rice portion alongside is well balanced and the vegetables cover fibre and vitamin C.

title: Chicken Tinola
description: A clear, gingery chicken broth with green papaya and spinach — gentle enough to be the first soup Filipino kids are given when they're sick or just hungry.

ingredients.note: bone-in thigh and leg pieces work well

ingredients.item: green papaya, peeled, seeded and cut into wedges
ingredients.note: or substitute chayote (sayote) if green papaya is unavailable

ingredients.item: fresh spinach or malunggay (moringa) leaves, stems trimmed

steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat; sauté the onion, garlic and ginger until softened and fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Add the chicken and cook, stirring occasionally, 5-7 minutes until the outside is lightly browned.
Pour in the fish sauce and cook 1-2 minutes to let the chicken absorb the flavour.
Add the water, bring to a boil, and skim off any foam; lower the heat, cover, and simmer 30-35 minutes until the chicken is fully cooked and tender.
Add the green papaya wedges and cook 3-5 minutes until just tender but still holding their shape.
Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Push the spinach or malunggay leaves into the broth and cook just until wilted, about 1 minute.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with rice, spooning extra broth over each bowl.
tips: Simmer the chicken low and slow rather than at a hard boil — this is what keeps the broth clean instead of cloudy.
Choose a firm, pale-green, underripe papaya; it holds its shape better than one that's starting to ripen.
kidNote: Shred the chicken off the bone for the 6-year-old's bowl to avoid small bones; the ginger flavour is mild enough that all three kids usually eat this without complaint.
nutritionNote: A light, mostly-broth dish that's naturally low in fat; pair with a modest scoop of rice and a side of fruit, since the soup itself is fairly light on calories and fibre beyond the papaya.

title: Bistek Tagalog
description: Thin-sliced beef marinated in calamansi and soy sauce, seared, then simmered with onions until the sauce turns savoury-tangy — a weeknight staple in Tagalog households.

ingredients.item: beef sirloin, thinly sliced against the grain

ingredients.note: or substitute lemon or lime juice

steps: Combine the beef with the calamansi juice, soy sauce, sliced onion, garlic and pepper; massage the marinade into the meat and let sit at least 30 minutes.
Lift the beef out of the marinade, squeezing off excess liquid; reserve the marinade, onions and garlic separately.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over high heat and sear the beef in batches, 1-2 minutes per side, until lightly browned; remove and set aside.
In the same pan, sauté the reserved marinated onions and garlic until softened.
Return the beef to the pan, pour in the reserved marinade and the water, and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer uncovered 8-10 minutes until the beef is tender and the sauce has reduced slightly.
Season with salt to taste, then turn off the heat and scatter the raw onion rings over the top; cover for 1-2 minutes so they soften in the residual heat.
Serve hot over steamed rice, spooning the sauce over both.
tips: Slice the beef thinly against the grain — this is what keeps bistek tender without needing a long braise.
The 30-minute marinate is mostly unattended; use the time to prep the rest of dinner.
Don't skip the raw onion rings on top; their bite against the savoury-sour sauce is the dish's signature.
nutritionNote: Protein-forward and moderately salty from the soy marinade; serve with extra steamed vegetables or a side salad and go easy on additional soy sauce at the table.

title: Pinakbet
description: Squash, eggplant, okra, long beans and bitter gourd simmered with a little pork and shrimp paste — the vegetable dish every Ilocano and Tagalog table has its own version of.

ingredients.note: or bagoong isda (fermented fish) for the more traditional Ilocano version

ingredients.item: kalabasa (squash), peeled and cut into chunks

steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat; sauté the onion and garlic until softened.
Add the pork and cook, stirring occasionally, until lightly browned at the edges.
Stir in the shrimp paste and cook 1-2 minutes until it deepens in colour and smells toasty.
Add the tomatoes and mash them into the mixture with the back of a spoon until softened and juicy.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then lower the heat, cover and simmer 15-20 minutes until the pork is tender.
Add the squash and cook about 2 minutes until almost tender.
Add the long beans and cook until tender-crisp, then add the bitter gourd, eggplant and okra.
Cook 4-5 minutes more until the vegetables are tender yet still hold their shape; season with salt and pepper and serve hot with rice.
tips: Add the vegetables in stages, hardest first, and stop cooking while they still have bite — overcooked pinakbet turns mushy and grey.
Salting the sliced ampalaya and rinsing it before cooking mellows its bitterness.
Resist stirring too often once the vegetables are in; a gentle toss keeps them from breaking apart.
kidNote: Bitter gourd is the vegetable most kids push aside — load each child's portion heavier on squash, long beans and eggplant, with just a token piece or two of ampalaya so they get used to the flavour without a full plate of it.
nutritionNote: An excellent fibre-rich, vegetable-forward dish that's lower in rice-displacing starch than most Filipino mains; the pork and shrimp paste add sodium, so skip extra patis or soy sauce at the table tonight.

title: Pancit Bihon
description: Rice noodles stir-fried with pork, shrimp and vegetables in a light soy broth until every strand is coated — the noodle dish served at birthdays for long life and luck.

ingredients.item: pork tenderloin or shoulder, thinly sliced

steps: Bring the chicken stock and soy sauce to a boil; add the rice noodles and soak off the heat for 1-2 minutes until softened, then drain, reserving the liquid.
Heat 1 teaspoon of the oil in a wok over medium-high heat; stir-fry the shrimp 1-2 minutes until pink, then remove and set aside.
Add the pork to the same wok and cook until lightly browned; remove and set aside with the shrimp.
Heat the remaining oil and sauté the onion and garlic until softened and fragrant.
Add the carrot and celery; stir-fry 30-40 seconds, then add the cabbage and cook until just tender-crisp.
Return the pork and shrimp to the wok, then add the softened noodles along with the reserved stock in splashes, tossing gently between additions.
Continue tossing until the noodles have absorbed the liquid and everything is evenly combined; season with salt and pepper to taste.
Transfer to a platter, scatter with green onions, and serve with calamansi halves for squeezing over.
tips: Add the stock to the noodles gradually, not all at once, so they finish tender rather than soggy or clumped.
Cut every vegetable to roughly the same thin size so the stir-fry cooks evenly in just a few minutes.
nutritionNote: Carb-heavy from the noodles with modest protein from pork and shrimp; load in extra cabbage and carrots and serve fruit on the side rather than additional rice.

title: Arroz Caldo
description: A thick, ginger-scented rice porridge with shredded chicken, topped with crispy garlic, egg and scallions — the standard Filipino sick-day and rainy-morning breakfast.

ingredients.note: or a whole chicken cut into pieces
mix half-and-half with regular rice for a looser porridge

steps: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat; sauté the onion, ginger and garlic until softened and fragrant.
Add the chicken and cook, stirring, until lightly browned on the outside.
Pour in the fish sauce and cook 1-2 minutes to let the chicken absorb the flavour.
Stir in the rice and cook 1-2 minutes, toasting it lightly in the aromatics.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, and skim off any foam; add the bouillon cubes and stir to dissolve.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer 30-35 minutes, stirring every few minutes so the rice doesn't stick, until the porridge thickens and the chicken is cooked through.
Shred or pull the chicken into bite-sized pieces if you like, then season with salt and pepper to taste.
Ladle into bowls and top with hard-boiled egg, fried garlic and green onions; serve with calamansi and extra fish sauce on the side.
tips: Stir every few minutes once the rice goes in — glutinous rice scorches on the bottom easily.
Fry the garlic bits separately and low and slow; they go from golden to burnt in seconds.
Leftover porridge thickens a lot in the fridge — loosen with a splash of hot water or stock when reheating.
nutritionNote: A soft, easy-to-digest rice porridge that's fairly plain on its own; the egg and shredded chicken supply protein, so add a side of sautéed vegetables since the dish itself offers little fibre.

title: Grilled Pork Belly
description: Pork belly slices marinated in calamansi, soy sauce and garlic, then grilled over charcoal and basted until charred at the edges — classic Filipino weekend backyard fare.

ingredients.item: pork belly, sliced into ½-inch thick slabs

steps: Combine the calamansi juice, fish sauce, garlic, chilies, brown sugar, salt and pepper in a bowl, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Add the pork belly slices and massage the marinade into the meat; cover and refrigerate at least 4 hours, or overnight for best flavour.
Meanwhile, mix all the dipping sauce ingredients together in a small bowl and set aside.
Drain the pork, reserving about 1 cup of the marinade; boil the reserved marinade 3-5 minutes to reduce, then stir in the oyster sauce and oil to make the basting sauce.
Prepare a hot charcoal or gas grill and lightly oil the grates; arrange the pork belly and grill 2-3 minutes per side to sear.
Continue grilling, basting regularly with the sauce once the pork loses its pink colour, 4-5 minutes per side more, until fully cooked and lightly charred.
Rest the pork for a few minutes off the heat, then slice into serving pieces.
Serve hot with the spiced vinegar dip and steamed rice.
tips: Marinate overnight if you can — it's unattended time and makes a real difference in flavour.
Keep a cooler part of the grill to move pieces to if the sugar in the marinade starts to burn before the pork is cooked through.
No charcoal grill? A ridged stovetop grill pan or the oven broiler both work — just watch the sugar for scorching.
kidNote: Set aside a few plain slices of pork belly before adding the chilies to the marinade so the kids get the same smoky-sweet flavour without any heat; keep the spiced vinegar dip strictly for the adults' table.
nutritionNote: Pork belly is high in fat, so balance the plate with a big side of grilled or steamed vegetables and a smaller rice portion rather than seconds of the meat.

title: Lumpiang Shanghai
description: Hand-rolled pork and vegetable spring rolls fried until crackling-crisp — the fixture of every Filipino birthday table and a favourite baon (packed lunch) treat.

ingredients.note: or ground chicken for a lighter version

ingredients.item: water chestnuts, drained and finely chopped
ingredients.note: 8 oz can; adds crunch, can omit if unavailable
thaw fully if frozen and keep covered with a damp cloth while working

steps: Combine the ground pork, green onions, water chestnuts, carrot, garlic, soy sauce, salt and pepper in a bowl and mix until evenly distributed.
Lay one spring roll wrapper on a flat surface with a corner pointing toward you, like a diamond.
Spoon about 1 heaping tablespoon of filling near the bottom corner and shape it into a thin log.
Fold the bottom corner over the filling, tuck and roll once, then fold in the side corners and continue rolling into a tight cylinder; seal the top corner with a dab of water.
Repeat with the remaining filling and wrappers, then cut each roll crosswise into 2-3 shorter pieces if you like.
Heat about 2 inches of oil in a deep pan to 165°C (330°F); fry the lumpia in batches, turning occasionally, 3-4 minutes until golden brown and crisp.
Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack.
Serve hot with sweet chilli sauce or banana ketchup for dipping.
tips: Roll tightly but don't overfill — an over-stuffed lumpia bursts open in the oil.
Uncooked rolls freeze well on a tray, then bag once solid; fry straight from frozen, adding a minute or two to the cook time.
Keep the oil at a steady medium heat; too hot browns the wrapper before the filling cooks through.
nutritionNote: Deep-fried and rich, so treat it as a portion-controlled side or party food rather than a main; pair with a vinegar-based dip instead of sweet sauce and add a vegetable soup or salad to the meal.

title: Fish in Coconut Milk
description: Pan-fried fish simmered in ginger-and-garlic coconut milk with eggplant, bok choy and a whole chili — a rich, warming way to stretch a market-fresh fish into dinner.

ingredients.item: whole galunggong (round scad) or tilapia fillets
ingredients.note: any firm white fish works; ask the market to gut and scale it

ingredients.item: seasoning granules or salt, for the fish
long green chili pepper (siling haba), left whole
ingredients.note: adds aroma more than heat; omit for a milder pot

steps: Season the fish with salt or seasoning granules and let sit 10 minutes.
Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in a pan and lightly fry the eggplant slices, about 2 minutes per side; set aside.
In the same pan, fry the seasoned fish in the remaining oil until golden and crisp on both sides; set aside.
Using about 3 tablespoons of the frying oil in a pot, sauté the ginger, garlic and onion until the onion softens and turns translucent.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring occasionally so it doesn't split.
Add the vinegar and simmer uncovered 3 minutes without stirring.
Season with fish sauce and pepper, then add the chili pepper and the fried fish; cover and simmer 3 minutes to let the fish absorb the sauce.
Add the bok choy, fried eggplant and malunggay leaves; cook 2 minutes more until the greens wilt and the sauce thickens slightly.
Transfer to a serving dish and serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Pan-frying the fish and eggplant first keeps them from falling apart once they hit the simmering coconut milk.
Let the coconut milk come to a boil before adding vinegar — this helps it stay smooth instead of curdling.
Leave the chili whole rather than slicing it if you want the flavour without real heat.
kidNote: Lift the whole chili pepper out before ladling the kids' portions, and check the fish carefully for small bones before serving it to the 6-year-old.
nutritionNote: Coconut milk makes this rich in saturated fat, so serve modest portions of the sauce over rice and pair with a plain vegetable side rather than doubling up on coconut-milk dishes in the same week.

title: Mung Bean Soup
description: Mung beans simmered until creamy, sautéed with tomato and garlic, and finished with pork cracklings and spinach — the humble Friday dinner Filipino families grew up on.

ingredients.item: dried mung beans (munggo), sorted and rinsed

ingredients.note: or crispy fried pork belly bits; omit and add a little extra oil for a vegetarian version

ingredients.item: fresh spinach or malunggay leaves, stems trimmed

steps: Sort through the mung beans, discarding any discoloured beans or debris, then rinse until the water runs clear.
Combine the beans and water in a pot; bring to a boil over medium heat, skimming off the foam that rises.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer 45-50 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beans are soft and starting to burst, topping up water if it drops much below 4 cups.
In a separate pan, heat the oil and sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant and softened.
Add the tomato and mash it into the mixture with a spoon until it breaks down into a light sauce.
Stir in the fish sauce and cook 1-2 minutes, then pour in the cooked mung beans with their liquid; bring back to a boil.
Add the chicharon and simmer a few minutes until it softens slightly in the broth; season with salt and pepper to taste.
Stir in the spinach, turn off the heat, and cover for 1-2 minutes until just wilted, then serve hot with rice.
tips: No need to soak the mung beans first — they cook through in under an hour from dry.
Add the chicharon just before serving if you want it to stay a bit crunchy rather than fully softened.
Mash a few extra spoonfuls of the cooked beans against the pot for a creamier, thicker soup.
nutritionNote: A genuinely balanced one-pot meal — mung beans bring plant protein, iron and fibre — so this is a good night to serve a smaller rice portion and let the beans and greens carry the plate.

title: Leche Flan
description: A silky steamed egg custard capped with soft caramel, unmolded glossy-side up — the sweet finale at every Filipino fiesta, birthday and Christmas table.
steps: Divide the sugar among 2-3 llanera moulds (or one large heatproof pan); set over low heat and tilt continuously until it melts into a light golden caramel, then remove from heat and swirl to coat the bottom evenly.
Set the caramel-lined moulds aside to cool and harden while you make the custard.
Whisk the egg yolks gently in a bowl, being careful not to incorporate too much air, since bubbles leave holes in the finished flan.
Stir in the condensed milk, evaporated milk, vanilla and salt, mixing in a slow circular motion until just combined.
Strain the mixture through a fine sieve into the prepared moulds to remove any stray bits of egg white or membrane.

Cover each mould tightly with foil and steam over gently simmering water for 30-40 minutes, or bake in a water bath at 190°C (375°F) for 50-60 minutes, until a toothpick inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 2 hours, or overnight, until fully set.
Run a thin knife around the edge and invert onto a plate so the caramel pools on top; slice and serve chilled.
tips: Strain the custard no matter how careful you were whisking — it's the difference between silky and eggy-textured flan.
Steaming over a gentle simmer, not a hard boil, prevents tiny air bubbles from pitting the surface.
Chilling overnight (unattended) firms the custard enough to unmould cleanly; don't rush this step.
nutritionNote: High in sugar and egg-yolk cholesterol, so treat this as an occasional dessert in modest slices rather than a daily one, and keep the rest of that meal lighter and vegetable-forward.
